newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean workers dodge paint to bust picket lines.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean workers dodge paint to bust picket lines.

text.p: Hyundai shipyard workers broke through picket lines on Wednesday, dodging fists and buckets of paint hurled by unionists to keep open South Korea's biggest dockyard and defy a call for nationwide strikes.
Several hundred strikers blocking the iron gates of the giant facility in the southeast city of Ulsan tossed yellow paint as non-union workers clad in blue overalls surged through.
Later, strike-breakers used bulldozers to smash down barricades at the shipyard entrance.
Cabinet ministers, meanwhile, said they would go ahead with the arrest of union leaders spearheading wildcat strikes over a new labour law railroaded through parliament on December 26.

Seizing leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions sheltering at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral "cannot be delayed", a statement from the Prime Minister's Office said, adding the government was ready for any backlash.

Seoul was largely unaffected by the nationwide strike call by the confederation and the officially-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions. Buses and subways were running normally, although some taxi drivers stayed at home.

The unions had called for the biggest strike ever in South Korea on Tuesday and Wednesday, intending to cap three weeks of sporadic stoppages over the law, which breaks a tradition of jobs-for-life by permitting layoffs.
President Kim Young-sam argues that flexible labour practices will cut corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.

The South Korean currency, the won, took a battering over fears that prolonged strikes could threaten already slowing export growth. The government sounded an alarm over the outlook for the trade deficit.
Trade Minister Ahn Kwang-koo warned that the stoppages, which have hurt firms crucial to the export-led economy, could make it harder for the country to control its snowballing trade deficit.
Last year's deficit is at $20 billion. Worries that the deficit could spin further out of control sent the won plunging to a new six-year low.
Stock investors, however, were relieved that the latest round of strikes was fizzling and sent share prices up for the second straight day.
In Ulsan, traditionally a hotbed of union militancy, blows were exchanged when non-union workers surged through the picket lines but there were no serious injuries.
The yard is part of the Hyundai Group. Its cranes, dry docks and welding plants were operating normally.
"Korea Telecom, the postal service and the nation's railroad services have not been influenced by the strike," a labour ministry official said.
Television showed commuters clambering on to buses, and subway trains pulling into stations even though 2,000 underground rail workers were on strike.
Operators of the Seoul subway have said non-union drivers could keep the system operating for two weeks.

The decision to go ahead with arrests of seven confederation leaders camped out in a ramshackle tent at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral was taken at a meeting of ministers presided over by Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung.
"The meeting confirmed the government's position that the arrest of the leaders of illegal strikes cannot be delayed even with some negative effects and repercussions," a ministry statement said.
The Labour Ministry said only three of Seoul's 88 bus companies had observed the strike call and bus services everywhere else were completely normal.
About a quarter of the nation's taxis were sitting idle in parking lots. Cab drivers have been the most enthusiastic supporters of the industrial action.
Finance Minister Han Seung-soo said strikes have cost the country 2.1 trillion won ($2.47 billion) in lost production and $400 million in lost exports.
